title: Kashmir and Jammu
capsule: The princely state of Jammu and Kashmir was created by the Treaty of Amritsar (1846) under which the British sold the Kashmir Valley to the Dogra chief Gulab Singh for 7.5 million Nanakshahi rupees after defeating the Sikh Empire in the First Anglo-Sikh War. The resulting state was an ethnically and religiously heterogeneous territory of roughly 220,000 sq km encompassing the Kashmir Valley (Muslim majority), Jammu (Hindu majority), Ladakh (Buddhist), and Gilgit-Baltistan. The princely state acceded to India in October 1947 — under disputed circumstances following the tribal invasion launched from Pakistan — triggering the First Indo-Pakistani War; the princely state as a constitutional entity effectively ended when the ceasefire line of 1 January 1949 divided it between Indian and Pakistani administration.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. External boundaries of the princely state are well documented by British survey; the 1947 ceasefire line that divided it is precisely recorded, though both India and Pakistan contest the territorial settlement to the present day.
